author: David Ogilvy
chunk_accuracy_note: The prior 6 chunks captured Ogilvy's major surface themes (headlines, brand image, research, the big idea, agency standards, honesty) but missed critical operational depth: the 10 client-selection criteria, 15 rules for being a good client, the 11 campaign commandments with specific research backing, the full new-business solicitation playbook, the typography/layout rules (14 specific items), the television commercial mechanics, the food/tourism/medicine category-specific commandments, and the career advancement protocol. The synthesis chunk about 'demand-capture stack' is a fabrication: Ogilvy never uses that phrase or frames his work that way. The chunk erroneously blends Sugarman and Halbert with Ogilvy as if they are one integrated framework when Confessions stands alone.
doctrine:
OGILVY'S OPERATING SYSTEM: Dense usable rules from direct text.

1. WHAT MAKES AN AD GOOD: One that sells the product without drawing attention to itself. Reader says 'I never knew that' not 'what a clever ad.' Professional duty is to conceal artifice.

2. THE PROMISE IS EVERYTHING: The content (what you say) beats the form (how you say it). The promise is the soul of the ad. Test promises against each other using mail-order-style split runs, matched consumer samples, and package-promise tests. Never guess the winning promise.

3. HEADLINE RULES (research-backed, not opinion):
   - 5x more people read the headline than body copy; headline = 80 cents of the dollar.
   - Write 16+ headline drafts per ad.
   - Flag your prospect in the headline (use BLADDER WEAKNESS if selling bladder remedy).
   - Every headline must promise a benefit or deliver news.
   - Most powerful words: FREE and NEW. Power words list: HOW TO, SUDDENLY, NOW, ANNOUNCING, INTRODUCING, AMAZING, SENSATIONAL, REVOLUTIONARY, STARTLING, MIRACLE, QUICK, EASY, BARGAIN, HURRY, LAST CHANCE.
   - Long headlines (10-18 words) with news and information outsell short headlines; no measurable difference between 12-word and 3-word readership.
   - Always include brand name in headline.
   - Never use negatives (reader misses the 'no').
   - No blind headlines that require body copy to decode.

4. BODY COPY RULES:
   - More facts = more sales. Never write short lazy ads.
   - Readership drops fast to 50 words then holds through 500 words; there is no penalty for long copy if it is interesting.
   - Always include testimonials; celebrity endorsements attract high readership.
   - Give helpful advice/service: hooks 75% more readers than product-only copy.
   - Write colloquially, as if answering a dinner-party question.
   - Avoid bombast, literary flourish, superlatives. Specific and factual beats general and puffed.
   - Never write copy you would not want your family to read.

5. ILLUSTRATION RULES:
   - Photographs sell more than drawings: more readers, more appetite appeal, more coupons.
   - 'Story appeal' (Harold Rudolph's term): inject mystery into photographs so readers want to know what happens next.
   - Babies attract women. Use sex-matched subjects for target audience.
   - Color doubles memorability.
   - No abstract art. No close-up faces. No crowd scenes. One dominant subject.
   - Captions are read 2x more than body copy: make each caption a miniature ad with brand name and promise.
   - Never overprint headline on illustration (reduces attention value 19%).
   - Design layout for the actual publication, not for a presentation board.

6. TYPOGRAPHY/LAYOUT (specific research rules):
   - Lower case outperforms ALL CAPS.
   - Serif type is easier to read than sans-serif.
   - Max 40 characters per column width.
   - Minimum 9-point type.
   - Keep opening paragraph to 11 words max.
   - Use subheads every 2-3 column inches.
   - Leading between paragraphs increases readership 12%.
   - Large initial letter increases readership 13%.
   - Never reverse type (white on black) or print over tint.
   - If using a coupon, top-center position pulls 80% more than bottom-outside.

7. TELEVISION RULES:
   - Pictures must tell the story; run the commercial silent to test it. If it doesn't sell mute, it is useless.
   - Max 90 words per minute.
   - Repeat the promise at least twice. Show it as a title/super.
   - Problem-solution-demonstration format sells 4x more than preaching.
   - Show product in first frame. Never stop selling.
   - Extreme close-ups only (TV screen too small for wide shots).
   - Avoid jingles; spoken word switches 3x more consumers.
   - No 'friendly word from our sponsor' lead-ins.

8. BRAND IMAGE DOCTRINE:
   - Every ad is a long-term investment in the brand symbol.
   - Brands with no consistent personality are 'wishy-washy neuters.'
   - Promotions are ephemeral; they create kinks in sales curves that make ad results unreadable.
   - 95% of campaigns are created ad hoc with no long-term image thinking. This is wrong.
   - Never be a copy-cat; no one has ever built a brand by imitating competitors.
   - Repeat a good ad until it stops pulling; sponsors tire of ads before the audience does.

9. CLIENT SELECTION (10 criteria, all must pass):
   (1) Product you are proud to advertise. Personal commitment required.
   (2) Believe you can do conspicuously better than current agency.
   (3) Avoid products with long-declining sales (usually intrinsic weakness).
   (4) Client must want the agency to make a profit.
   (5) If unprofitable, must give chance to create remarkable advertising.
   (6) Must be able to live happily with the client personally.
   (7) Advertising must be central to their marketing mix, not marginal.
   (8) No pre-launch products unless bundled with an established product.
   (9) Never take associations as clients: too many masters, too little money.
   (10) Never accept accounts contingent on hiring a specific individual.

10. 15 RULES TO BE A GOOD CLIENT (the client side):
    (1) Emancipate your agency from fear; frightened agencies cannot produce good work.
    (2) Select the right agency by interviewing principals over dinner, not by spec pitches.
    (3) Brief the agency thoroughly; the more they know, the better the work.
    (4) Do not compete with the agency in the creative area.
    (5) Coddle the goose that lays golden eggs; launching new products is expert, expensive work.
    (6) Don't strain advertising through too many approval levels; committees kill campaigns.
    (7) Make sure your agency makes a profit; pay a flat fee, not just 15% commission.
    (8) Don't haggle over bills; stinginess on research means flying blind.
    (9) Be candid about what is wrong; don't threaten, but be direct.
    (10) Set high standards; demand home runs, praise when they happen.
    (11) TEST EVERYTHING. TEST is the most important word in advertising.
    (12) Hurry; time is a profit variable. Lambert reviewed Listerine monthly and made $25M in 8 years.
    (13) Don't waste time on problem babies; back your winners.
    (14) Tolerate genius even when it is disagreeable.
    (15) Don't underspend; a ticket three-quarters of the way to Europe gets you nowhere.

11. NEW BUSINESS PLAYBOOK:
    - Pick blue-chip targets on day one and pursue them relentlessly over years.
    - Escape obscurity fast: trade press relationships, calculated speeches (max 2/year) designed to provoke maximum stir, friends in adjacent professions, frequent direct mail to 600 key people.
    - Speculative research presentations (survey the prospect's problem before you pitch) win accounts.
    - Sometimes refusing to prepare a spec campaign wins accounts (KLM).
    - Never get an account so big you cannot afford to lose it: fear destroys candor.
    - Never compete publicly when more than 4 other agencies are involved.
    - Make solo presentations; one conductor is more memorable than one orchestra.
    - Always disclose your flaws voluntarily: antique dealers who show defects win trust.
    - Reject 59 accounts per year; selectivity signals quality and inflames desire.

12. AGENCY MANAGEMENT:
    - Head of agency's primary job: create atmosphere in which creative mavericks can do useful work.
    - The head must still do occasional creative work to prove the hand has not lost its cunning.
    - Praise rarely so it is treasured when given.
    - Fire incompetents; it demoralizes professionals to work beside amateurs.
    - Keep offices shipshape; messiness creates sloppiness and leads to lost documents.
    - Avoid nepotism, toadies, paper-warriors, and quarrelsome executives.
    - Hire subordinates who are good enough to succeed you.
    - Annual all-hands meeting (transparent, profits included) builds 49,700-person rooter network.
    - Delegate but do not withdraw; over-delegation produces mediocrity.

13. ADVERTISING ETHICS AND ECONOMICS:
    - Informative factual advertising is more effective AND more ethical than puffery: academic virtue and commercial self-interest march together.
    - Advertising cannot foist an inferior product: it can persuade people to try once; they never buy again.
    - Aggressive promotion of a bad product kills it faster.
    - Advertising lowers prices by enabling scale.
    - Political advertising is the ultimate vulgarity; Ogilvy refused all political accounts.
contradictions: The OS 'Maximum-by-default' rule pushes maximum creative depth on every output. Ogilvy explicitly warns against this instinct: committees and over-effort without research backing produce mediocre work. The discipline is: research first, then creative, not creative maximalism without measurement.

The OS uses 'Repetition > Novelty' as a creative rule. Ogilvy's version is narrower and more precise: repeat a good ad until it stops pulling in the market, but internally keep developing reserve campaigns and never run the same creative just because the client is tired of it. The principle is measured market fatigue, not general repetition doctrine.

The synthesis chunk in the prior distillation invents a 'demand-capture stack' that fuses Ogilvy with Halbert and Sugarman. Ogilvy never uses this framing. His system is promise-led and research-validated, not a linear funnel stack. The fusion flattens his research discipline into generic copywriting doctrine.

Ogilvy is strongly anti-jingle and anti-entertainment in advertising. Any OS creative direction that privileges entertainment value (spectacle, mythology, aesthetic gravity) in client-facing work contradicts Ogilvy's core finding: there is zero correlation between people liking a commercial and being sold by it.

OS photography doctrine may overweight visual sophistication (Meisel/Roversi lane, restraint, quiet luxury). Ogilvy's research-backed finding: the technically 'beautiful' photographs that win camera-club awards do NOT work in advertisements. Story appeal (curiosity, 'what happens next') outperforms aesthetic elegance.
gate_candidates: Before any copy ships: does the headline promise a specific benefit or deliver news, and does it include the brand name?
Before any illustration is finalized: does it have story appeal (does a viewer ask 'what happens next?'), and is it a photograph not a drawing?
Before any campaign is approved internally: have at least two versions of the core promise been tested against each other?
workflow_candidates: Promise-selection research protocol: distribute product with different promise statements on packaging, compare repeat-order rates; or show promise cards to consumers and measure selection preference before writing a single headline.

New-business escape-from-obscurity sequence: (1) trade-press lunch and relationship, (2) two calculated speeches per year designed for maximum stir, (3) adjacent-profession network cultivation, (4) direct-mail progress reports to 600 key targets, (5) speculative research on top target before pitching.
notes: This is one of the highest-density practitioner manuals in the OS corpus. The prior chunk count of 6 concepts was severely under-extracted. The real doctrine count is 13+ distinct operating systems, each with numbered sub-rules. Every claim is grounded in named research (Gallup, Starch, Rudolph, Hopkins precedents, mail-order split runs). The book is not a manifesto or framework: it is a practitioner's operations manual with specific rules that can be applied directly to SNIPED copy, photography caption strategy, client selection, and outreach design. The contradictions with the OS visual doctrine (beauty vs. story appeal) are material and should be surfaced before any aesthetic-first creative decisions.
